title: Spreading brass, closing saxophones and flatted fifths
summary: Smith explains scoring above the lead, placing flatted fifths in the middle, and spacing brass wider than saxophones.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Would you ever score an instrument above the lead?
Mmm-hmm.

In other words, would it ever happen that you'd give... If the lead instrument would be a trumpet playing the melody, would you ever score a third or a fourth above that for one of the other instruments to get a special effect?
Yeah. But it wouldn't be no heavy instrument.
It has to be a clarinet or a...
It got to be a clarinet or a flute, something like that. Then you'd get that effect, and it would sound all right.
When you were making arrangements, would you incorporate quite sophisticated harmonies? Would you use augmenteds or flattened fifths or things like that?

Flatted fifths? No. It was going with the chords, what effect I wanted to get out of that. Whatever I wanted the chord to sound like. In other words, them flatted fifths and things were mostly going to be in the middle somewhere. Yeah, you've got to put them in the middle.
Well, it might be the second instrument.
Mmm-hmm. Yeah. And the saxophones are the only ones that you can write, put them close together, and they're on(?). They wanted to have the (?) run together and make it
Buster Smith - 147
sound funny. You can do that with the saxophone, but you can't do that with the trumpet, the brass...
You have to split the brass up.
You have to spread them out.
When you say spread them out, do you mean spread them out at least a third?
Yeah. Right.
For instance, with saxophones, can you score saxophones so they'd be, like, even seconds apart as opposed to thirds? Or fourths?

Well, yeah, according to how you want the chord to sound. The effect you want to get out of it. Sometimes you had an alto, and you might be playing a little more notes. He might be playing some eighth notes, while the middle horns, the third also and tenor, would be playing some quarter notes, and he's playing double notes...
Double time.
Yeah. In other words, you pass them and make them (?) like you're walking on a chord going up -- going up, like da-da-de-de-de-de... You see them older guys playing quarter notes walking...
Right. One-two-three-four.
Yeah, walking right up behind it. Staying right with it. Yeah. But you're going to have a right note, a (?)
Buster Smith - 148

like that, or what you (?) most is the whole band, and they'll all be standing still on a chord, but you got so many of them in there and you got 'em fitted(?) there, so it will fit right where, if he's making that sound...and it will fit right in, because he'll be making some contrapuntal notes up there.
Right. In the (?) clef.
Yeah. But it will sound right when you get it up... You end up where you start...
[PAUSE]
